title: Gandhi and Charlie Chaplin: Who Is the Machine For? — The 1931 London Encounter
summary: When Chaplin questioned Gandhi's opposition to modern machinery, Gandhi illuminated that he did not oppose technology itself, but an economic machine that deprives millions of livelihoods to enrich a few oligarchs.
keywords: Gandhi and Charlie Chaplin: Who Is the Machine For? — The 1931 London Encounter
full_text:
On September 22, 1931, in the working-class neighborhood of Canning Town in East London, two of the most recognizable men on Earth met in the modest home of Dr. Katial. On one side stood Mahatma Gandhi, leader of India's non-violent independence struggle; on the other stood Charlie Chaplin, the legendary silent cinema master whose 'Little Tramp' embodied the dignity of the common working man.

Chaplin had long admired Gandhi's moral courage. Yet one burning question puzzled the cinematic artist: Why did Gandhi oppose industrialization and modern machinery so vehemently?

As they sat down together, Chaplin broached the subject with genuine curiosity:
"Mr. Gandhi, why are you so opposed to modern machinery? Doesn't machinery emancipate human beings from backbreaking drudgery? Doesn't it offer mankind leisure, efficiency, and material abundance?"

Gandhi looked at Chaplin with a twinkle in his eyes and smiled softly:
"My dear Chaplin! The world has misunderstood my stance. I am not against machinery in the abstract. But look at India.
We are a nation of three hundred million people. For six months of the year, our agricultural peasantry has no work. 
The vast mechanical textile mills of Manchester destroyed the spinning wheels of our villages. A single great steam loom can do the work of a hundred villagers in an instant. The mill owner in London gets enormously wealthy; but what becomes of the hundred Indian families who lose their livelihood? They starve! They are reduced to beggary!"

Chaplin listened intently to Gandhi's socio-economic logic. He then pressed further:
"Gandhiji! If working hours were reduced, if workers were guaranteed adequate leisure, and if the wealth generated by machines were equitably shared among all who work, would you then support machinery?"

Gandhi's eyes lit up as he replied emphatically:
"Most certainly! The machine must be the servant of man, never his master. When a machine concentrates wealth in the hands of a few and creates widespread unemployment, it is an instrument of violence. When it relieves human misery and uplifts the community equally, it is a blessing!"

Chaplin was deeply moved. The conversation crystallized the themes that had long troubled the filmmaker's conscience. 

Five years later, in 1936, Chaplin released his crowning masterpiece, **Modern Times**, depicting the Little Tramp swallowed whole by the massive turning gears of a factory assembly line. When audiences across the globe laughed and cried at Chaplin's biting satire of industrial exploitation, they were witnessing the artistic embodiment of the very truth Gandhi had articulated in that London parlor: "Is the machine for man, or is man for the machine?"
moral: Gandhi's insight—that technology must serve humanity rather than enslave workers—stands as a prophetic critique echoing into today's age of artificial intelligence and automation.
witty_quote: If machinery provided leisure, shortened toil, and ensured the equitable distribution of wealth to all, I would welcome it with open arms. But when it turns millions of human beings into unemployed paupers, resistance is a moral duty!

options: If it guaranteed leisure, reduced toil, and equitably distributed wealth to all workers

If machines only ran on water
quiz.hint: Gandhi explicitly stated he welcomed machinery if it served human welfare, provided leisure, and shared wealth fairly.
